item.title: NASA chief says if China beats us to moon, 'I'll be fired' | Exclusive - USA Today
item.description:
NASA chief says if China beats us to moon, 'I'll be fired' | Exclusive

As NASA accelerates its Artemis program with launches of more than 20 crewed and uncrewed moon-base missions, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman looks forward to a parallel wave of private space-company investment powering up Florida's Space Coast within the next five years: "You're going to see very big rockets launching nearly all the time."

"It will be such a spaceport," Isaacman told FLORIDA TODAY, part of the USA TODAY Network, during a one-on-one interview, drawing contrast with sluggish activity after the end of NASA's shuttle era.

"We now have such demand for every parcel of land here and every launch pad because of the opportunity that's being presented to us across this great frontier. You're going to see Starships launching all the time. You're going to see Blue Origins launching all the time," Isaacman said.

"You’ll see Stoke launching all the time. You're going to see Relativity launching all the time. You're still going to have SLS launches probably every year as we continue to send astronauts to the moon. So it's going to be a lot of activity around here," he said.

Isaacman dropped by the FLORIDA TODAY blockhouse at the KSC Press Site on Friday, Oct. 23, for an interview after delivering a series of Artemis III updates during a NASA news conference. The agency is targeting summer 2027 to launch the Artemis III crew into low-Earth orbit.

Conducted in tandem with Blue Origin and SpaceX, this lunar-lander test mission should pave the way for the Artemis IV crew to venture to the moon in 2028, returning Americans to the rugged lunar surface for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972.

Isaacman revealed the outline of the on-orbit Artemis III mission, which should last 14 to 17 days. The four astronauts and their Orion spacecraft will lift off atop NASA's 322-foot Space Launch System, then dock with and board the crew cabin of Blue Origin's Mark 2 lander — which is manufactured at Lunar Plant 1 at the company's ever-growing Rocket Park campus on Merritt Island.

Afterward, the Orion will dock with the nose cone of SpaceX's Starship human-habitation lander for about two hours, but the astronauts will not board. A Starship reached orbit for the first time in September during its 14th test flight from Starbase in Texas, and SpaceX has released scant details about lander development.

Isaacman views NASA's new race to the moon as a U.S. geopolitical goal, as rivals China and Russia plan to develop a nuclear-reactor-powered moon base within a decade. He said it is imperative to accelerate the Artemis timeline after NASA bogged down for decades in what he describes as "layers of process and bureaucratic inertia and endless deliberation."

NASA's liftoffs of Artemis I (Nov. 16, 2022) and Artemis II (April 1, 2026) were separated by 1,232 days — or nearly 3½ years.

“I'm saying we need to launch a big rocket at least once a year. So we have to launch in ’27. Artemis III must fly. And we have to get data back from the integrated tests with the Blue Origin lander," Isaacman told FLORIDA TODAY.

"I mean, that is critical. Without that, you can't move on to IV. Because you're going to learn something. And you're going to learn something that's going to change hardware, that's gonna change training and procedures. So that mission must fly in '27," he said.

NASA's goal: Beat China to the moon

The U.S. Senate confirmed Isaacman as NASA's 15th administrator in December 2025. The Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University graduate and Shift4 founder previously funded and commanded SpaceX's Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn crewed missions in low-Earth orbit.

During a January 2026 FLORIDA TODAY interview, Isaacman said, "I hope there’s 50 more Artemis missions to follow," after Artemis I lifts off. Then in March 2026, he announced NASA's Gateway lunar space station development was paused indefinitely in lieu of building a $20-billion-plus moon base near the lunar south pole.

"People look at the moon, and they’re like, 'Wow, it's a big moon. Isn't it enough for all of us?' The south pole (is) critical. That south pole is the size of Washington, DC. That is your training ground, with the water ice in those craters to prepare for Mars. We know that. The Chinese know that," Isaacman said.

"They get their landers there first, it's first-come first-serve — and could actually deny our ability to learn in the most critical environment that’s been gifted to us, three days away, before we eventually continue on our journey to Mars," he said.

Chinese officials aim to launch their first taikonauts to the lunar surface by 2030. FLORIDA TODAY asked Isaacman what would change at NASA if China sets foot on the moon before the United States.

"What if you do come up short? Does that mean there should be change? Absolutely there should be change. The good news is, we've been implementing that already. That's what I said the first couple weeks on the job. 'Hey, you know, if the Chinese beat us back to the moon, I'll be fired,'" Isaacman said.

"So I'll be watching on TV as Congress hauls all of the major contractors before Congress and says, 'Where'd the $100 billion go? What happened over all these decades? How could we let this happen when we've been working on it and we did it before?' And those are very fair questions," he said.

"But we're not waiting to that point. We're implementing change. We're rebuilding core competencies, bringing the workforce back in-house — the organic capabilities to do things like you would expect of your space agency," he said.

NASA bringing talent in-house ahead of moon landing

Across the country, NASA is insourcing thousands of contract employees through at least the end of 2026 — KSC officials posted a video Sept. 21 showing nearly 600 new NASA civil servants taking oaths of office.

In late August, NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley hosted its largest swearing-in ceremony since its inception nearly 87 years ago. On the Space Coast, Florida Department of Commerce WARN mass-layoff notices generated Central Florida news headlines when Amentum announced 70 layoffs and Aetos Systems announced up to 126 terminations at KSC.

Isaacman said it is key to note that as contractors provide notice because they are winding down some resources, "NASA is probably taking them all, or nearly all of them."

"What this is about is restoring core competencies and organic capabilities to your space agency. It's not about a reduction of workforce. It’s about bringing the workforce in-house. Why is that important? We need to be agile," Isaacman said.

Since NASA's shuttle era, Isaacman said 75% of the agency workforce was staffed via contractors: "Not through one company. Dozens and dozens of subcontractors."

As an example, he said if NASA needs to move 100 people for 90 days to Alabama to do welding work for United Launch Alliance Centaur V upper-stages for future Artemis missions, it comprises a contracting process between three companies.

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, NASA officials shared photos of the massive Artemis III SLS core stage and solid rocket boosters stacked and vertical inside the towering Vehicle Assembly Building at KSC.

"In the business of launching a complicated rocket with 8.8 million pounds of thrust, you cannot let those skills atrophy," Isaacman said.

"So it's imperative that we launch in 2027 to continue to exercise those 'big-rocket muscles,'" he said.

Asked what worries or concerns him most about the complex hardware and systems required for the Artemis IV moon landing, Isaacman said it is very easy to gravitate to the lunar lander. But in addition, he pointed out "a lot of things in motion," such as the lighter spacesuit under development by Axiom Space and ULA developing a "stretch" Centaur V. This SLS upper stage will boast 50% more propellant capacity than a typical Centaur to push the Orion into a lower lunar orbit.

"Everybody within our organization, our agency, needs to be building and needs to be doing it constantly so it all converges at the right time," Isaacman said.

"Because it is hard. It's difficult. And yes, any one piece along the way breaks us," he said.

Rick Neale  is a Space Reporter at FLORIDA TODAY, where he has covered news since 2004. Contact Neale at Rneale@floridatoday.com . Twitter/X:  @RickNeale1

item.title: 3 minutes of fear: Artemis II commander recalls the moment he thought he'd be lost in space forever - Live Science
item.description:
TENERIFE, Spain — The commander of NASA's Artemis II mission briefly feared that he and his crew would never return home from their trip around the moon after overshooting their turn-back point.

Commander Reid Wiseman and his three crewmates were supposed to reach 219,667 nautical miles (252,788 standard miles, or 406,823 kilometers) — farther than any humans have ever traveled from their home planet — before turning back toward Earth on the sixth day of their 10-day mission to the moon.

But the odometer on the Integrity spacecraft continued to tick upward as they shot past their intended point of return, leading the astronaut to fear that something had gone terribly wrong, he told an audience here at the Starmus VIII festival earlier this week. (This semi-annual event is held to celebrate achievements in science, exploration, and creativity.)

"Mission control in Houston had told us our maximum distance would be 219,667 nautical miles and that was the furthest we were supposed to be from Earth," Wiseman said. "I was watching this number, and I saw it hit 219,667, and I thought, 'Great, this is the farthest we will be from Earth, and the next number I will see will be 219,666 ‪—‬ we'll be going home.' But about three minutes later, I didn't see 219,666; I saw 219,668. It went up. I was like. 'Huh? That's weird.'

Artemis II astronauts Jeremy Hansen, Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman were presented with the Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Spain, on Oct. 17.

"And then about three minutes later, it goes to 219,669, and that was the moment that I felt real fear because I thought we had just gone too far ‪—‬ we're never going to come home ‪—‬ and so I was very scared," he added.

Then, at last, he saw the counter start to drop. Meanwhile, NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Christina Koch were at the window, doing science observations of the moon, and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen was sending reports back to mission control ‪—‬ so Wiseman's moment of terror went unnoticed.

When Wiseman saw the odometer click back to 219,668 nautical miles, he said, "We're going home," and the crew let out a cheer. "I knew there was a good chance we might make it," he added.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In an interview with Live Science's sister publicationThe Week Junior Science+Nature, Wiseman paid tribute to NASA's Earth-based teams for the ultimate success of the mission.

"Getting home safely is a testament to the engineering rigor and the flight control teams back here on planet Earth, who put this rocket together and then who controlled it as we went out to the moon and came back. Those are the true heroes of this mission. They have real courage."

The Artemis II mission launched from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 1. It was the first crewed flight of the Orion space capsule and the first crewed mission to travel to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, taking nearly 10 days to fly around the lunar far side and return to Earth.

Nearly every moment of the crew's activities in the Orion capsule was livestreamed to the world, garnering massive public interest in the mission. The Artemis II crewmembers were awarded the Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication at the Starmus VIII festival.

item.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission - Space
item.description:
TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission.

"If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife.

The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth, giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon. Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward.

"Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. "Because we were getting so low."

The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites.

"The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained.

It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn.

"So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said.

The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon, or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled.

The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era.

Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing, the warning turned out to be a false alarm.

So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon.

"We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled.

"Everything is tracking. It's looking good."

Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph).

Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon.

The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

item.title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026.

“Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.”

During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before.

“It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.”

After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments.

“I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.”

Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Serving as Center Management Authority for JPL mission execution, Wiseman will ensure operational excellence across mission support functions in accordance with NASA requirements and applicable federal and state regulations. In addition, he will be JPL’s primary interface for national security programs.

“Reid brings to Caltech and JPL a truly unprecedented view of what humanity can achieve when ingenuity and determination are matched with the courage to pursue the furthest frontiers,” said Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana. “His pioneering spirit coupled with unbounded curiosity make him a natural fit for Caltech and JPL, a force-multiplier for a community whose daring continues to push the limits of humanity’s reach. I look forward to working closely with Dave and Reid as we chart our next era of exploration in partnership with NASA, elevating America’s space ambitions to breathtaking new heights.”

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Wiseman joined the Navy, going on to fly combat missions and serve as a test pilot. He also has a master’s degree in systems engineering from Johns Hopkins University in his hometown of Baltimore.

item.title: Artemis II crew talks to ABC News from space: Their journey so far and what's ahead - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
item.description:
Artemis II crew talks to ABC News from space: Their journey so far and what's ahead

From toilet fixes to Earth views, the four astronauts detail the mission so far.

The Artemis II mission launched on Wednesday, taking four astronauts on a historic, 10-day mission around the moon and giving them views of a lifetime along the way.

A day after lift-off, ABC News' Gio Benitez spoke with astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen from their Orion spacecraft about the journey so far, and what they are anticipating for the days ahead.

"I don't know what we all expected to see ... but you could see the entire globe, from pole to pole," Commander Wiseman said of the crew's view of Earth from space Thursday.

"You could see Africa, Europe, and if you looked really close, you could see the northern lights. It was the most spectacular moment, and it paused all four of us in our tracks," he added.

This mission marks the first time humans have flown beyond low-Earth orbit since the Apollo 17 mission that landed on the moon in 1972.

The crew is going on a 685,000-mile journey around the moon, also known as a lunar fly-by.

The launch on Wednesday was seen around the world, as the crew successfully lifted off at 6:35 p.m. ET from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Hansen, mission specialist and part of the Canadian Space Agency, said that even though they were all expecting it, when the rocket boosters actually lit up and they left the launch pad, "there's just a moment of disbelief."

"The fact that we launched -- it just totally takes you by surprise, even though you're expecting it, at least for me anyway, and just had a huge smile across my face," he said.

Koch, a mission specialist who holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman at 328 days, addressed the toilet issue onboard the spacecraft, which was reported after launch.

"I'm proud to call myself the space plumber," Koch said. "I like to say that it is probably the most important piece of equipment on board."

Crew members said at the time that the Orion capsule's toilet, dubbed the Universal Waste Management System, had a blinking fault light while they tested it, but it had been resolved since.

"So we were all breathing a sigh of relief when it turned out to be just fine," Koch said.

Glover, the mission pilot who will make history as the first person of color to go to the moon, said from high Earth orbit, the divisions of Earth are far out of view.

"Trust us, you look amazing, you look beautiful," he said of Earth. "You also look like one thing. Homo sapiens is all of us, no matter where you're from or what you look like. We're all one people."

"We call amazing things that humans do 'moonshots' for a reason, because this brought us together and showed us what we can do when we not just put our differences aside, when we bring our differences together and use all the strengths to accomplish something great," Glover said.

Before speaking with ABC News on Thursday, the Artemis II crew successfully completed a critical milestone in the mission, the translunar injection burn that boosted the Orion spacecraft out of Earth’s orbit onto a trajectory toward the moon.

During a press conference after the maneuver, Lori Glaze, acting associate administrator at NASA, said that the translunar injection burn was "flawless."

“From this point forward, the laws of orbital mechanics are going to carry our crew to the moon, around the far side and back to Earth,” Glaze said.

item.title: NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images

NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study.

More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images.

When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface.

Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide. Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond.

item.title: 'Dude! No way!' Scientists jump for joy over Artemis II moon science results - Space
item.description:
We have our first look at the science from Artemis II, and it's as amazing as we might have hoped.

This past April, four astronauts strapped in for a flyby around the moon and back to Earth. The first mission to the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972, this success marked an incredible historic milestone. The Artemis II crew also conducted groundbreaking science, observing parts of the moon no human had ever laid eyes on before. And now, we have our first look at some of the science from the mission.

"It's the science community's job now to take these data and go do magical things with it," David Hollibaugh Baker, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during a Wednesday (10/7) press conference that announced the mission's initial science results.

This is just the first batch of data from the mission, but it includes a whopping 996 new images, 814 GB of observations and 521 minutes of audio from the crew that has never been heard before. Everything from that astronauts' handwritten notes and drawings to photographs and verbal observations have revealed exciting new information — about impact flashes on the moon, for example, as well as the terminator line between the lunar "day" and "night" sides and a whole range of lunar colors and observations from beyond the mysterious far side.

Let's take a quick look at some of the highlights.

Impact flashes

"Dude, no way!" Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman of NASA exclaimed in newly released mission audio.

"It's just like a 'bloop!'" mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency added as the flashes appeared on the lunar surface. .

As Artemis II's Orion capsule flew by the moon, the four astronauts onboard — Wiseman, Hansen and NASA astronauts Victor Glover (mission pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist)— started seeing flashes of light on the lunar surface. These were impact flashes caused by small rocks hitting the lunar surface and vaporizing in the impact.

"We have seen three impact flashes so far," Wiseman said to Mission Control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. "It was not sun glint off a particulate from the thrusters or the purge tanks. It was definitely impact flashes on the moon."

"Amazing news," Mission Control responded. "I literally just looked over at the SER [Science Evaluation Room], and they were jumping up and down, literally."

In total, the crew saw five impact flashes on the moon's surface, which the mission's science team was able to confirm didn't come from other sources.

While the Artemis II crew was equipped with cameras, they were also trained to make observations with the unaided eye. And impact flashes happen too quickly to photograph them, so — as you can see above — the crew used a tablet to make annotations and describe their observations.

"We wanted them to look visually, so there are not camera images of that, but we have their annotations of when they saw them," Jennifer Heldmen, science theme lead for the Artemis II mission, said during the briefing.

A rainbow moon

In addition to seeing impact flashes across the lunar surface, the Artemis II crew observed a wide range of colors on the moon.

Looking up in the night sky, it might seem that the moon is just shades of gray. But as the astronauts saw during their flyby, the moon is gray, black, brown, tan, white, green and even blue. This muted rainbow of colors was not only visually striking, as the astronauts' photos show, but it can also help scientists determine what types of rocks and minerals might be found in different regions across the moon's surface.

"The crew reported greens and yellowish hues on top of Aristarchus Plateau, signaling they were seeing remnants of different styles and epochs of volcanic activity, and the crew contrasted those colors to nearby browns and grays of adjacent volcanic plains," Ariel Deutsch, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during the briefing, givingone example of these colorful observations.

"To me, it's primarily like a brownish-green glass, and then if I went up into the mares [dark volcanic deposits] to the north of Aristarchus, I would give that a very muted brown," Wiseman said in mission recordings shared in this release.

"It's like a jaundiced cheek of the moon," Koch remarked in mission audio, describing yellowish colors on the moon.

And while the crew took some amazing photographs of the moon, in this data release we can also see their handwritten notes annotating the colors they saw on the moon.

The far side of the moon

As the moon is tidally locked to Earth, it has one "day side" that always faces us and one far or "night side" that is always facing away. When the Artemis II astronauts flew by the moon, they flew around the entire object, even around the far side. During their flyby, they were able to see a part of the far sidethat has never been observed up close like this before.

"The Artemis II crew were the first people to see this section of the moon illuminated in all of human history," Alex Stoken, a member of the Crew Lunar Observations team, said during the briefing.

When they approached the moon's far side, the crew also came upon the terminator line, or the boundary between the day and night sides of the moon.

At the terminator, the team was able to view the incredible contrasting shadows and textures of the lunar surface, revealing sharp details about the moon's topography.

"The terminator is the most striking thing that I’ve seen so far," Glover said as the crew flew by.

As they rounded the moon's far side, the moon was backlit by the sun, essentially eclipsing it. This allowed for incredibly unique and sharp views of the moon.

"You’ve got to be kidding me," Koch said in the capsule. "You can actually see mountains."

These are just a few highlights from this incredibly thorough and detailed data release. As we dig deeper into this initial science, you can take a dive through the data yourself here and here.

item.title: Artemis II Heat Shield After Splashdown - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Shortly after NASA’s Artemis II mission splashed down on April 10, 2026, U.S. Navy divers captured underwater imagery of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield. In the months after, the agency measured whether the thermal protection system effectively safeguarded the crew and Orion systems as the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere. This rigorous analysis confirmed that the heat shield performed as expected.

Image credit: US Navy

item.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface.

Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected.

In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection system effectively safeguarded the crew and Orion systems as the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere. This test flight was the first time astronauts flew aboard Orion.

Orion reached a maximum velocity of 39 times the speed of sound and experienced external temperatures exceeding 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit at its peak, all while the four astronauts inside Orion stayed relatively cool with a cabin temperature in the mid-70 degree Fahrenheit range during their return to Earth from the Moon.

After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings, informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. Analysis prior to the mission showed that limiting downrange distance would limit how long the spacecraft’s heat shield spent in the temperature range at which the Artemis I heat shield phenomenon occurred.

The spacecraft reentered with precision, entering within only 192 feet of its targeted entry interface, and successfully splashed down only 0.59 miles from the predicted landing site off the coast of San Diego. Initial inspections of the thermal protection system, including diver imagery of the spacecraft’s heat shield taken just after splashdown and further inspections on the recovery ship, found it performed as expected, with a significant reduction in the amount of cracks and char loss as compared to Artemis I.

Upon the spacecraft’s return to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida after the Moon mission, thermal protection system experts began additional examination of the heat shield, made of 186 unique blocks of an ablative material called Avcoat. The heat shield was then transported to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where work on sample extraction and internal x-ray scans began in August to provide further engineering insight into the system and behavior of the material.

A thorough post-flight assessment review found that Orion’s aerodynamic and aerothermal performance, including the heat shield and backshell thermal protection system, was in line with engineering predictions based on pre-flight analyses and ground testing. The shorter allowable down range during entry reduced the cracking and char loss experienced on the Artemis II heat shield relative to the Artemis I heat shield by a factor of ten, proving the effectiveness of the trajectory modification. Engineers found only nine spots of char loss of varying sizes on the Artemis II heat shield dish, compared to 103 during Artemis I.

The analysis also showed that Orion’s robust heat shield design showed consistency from Artemis I to Artemis II, evident by the performance of system features such as the seams between the heat shield Avcoat blocks and the Avcoat surrounding the heat shield compression pad separation bolts.

Post-flight inspection of Orion’s backshell, the protective cover on the sloped sides of the crew module made up of 1,300 ceramic tiles, showed expected performance across the crew module surface. Visual inspections indicated backshell features designed to seal and protect penetrations such as windows, vents, thrusters, and the side hatch also met expectations, with no signs of overheating observed.

The team also performed post-flight laser scans of the heat shield surface and is comparing this data to pre-flight measurements to determine material recession, which will then be compared to analysis predictions. Engineers are continuing with heat shield sample extraction at NASA Marshall and subsequent material test and assessment and thermal analysis, to support long-term heat shield development, manufacturing efforts, and data capture.

Orion’s performance and the team’s analysis on Artemis II reflect system robustness, capability to support crew, and critical insights gathered that will enhance the Artemis III mission and beyond. Following the extensive Artemis I heat shield investigation, upgrades were made to the heat shield design for Artemis III to achieve uniformity and consistent permeability of the Avcoat blocks. Technicians attached the heat shield for the Artemis III Orion crew module at NASA Kennedy in early July, and the Orion crew and service modules were joined at the end of July. The spacecraft has since been successfully powered up for the first time, enabling engineers to check all connection lines between the two modules are working as planned.

NASA continues to advance toward Artemis III as teams ready the Orion spacecraft for next year’s mission in low Earth orbit. NASA will launch the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft with NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) Luca Parmitano, to rendezvous with human lander test articles from Blue Origin and SpaceX to demonstrate critical systems and operations needed for future lunar landings, beginning with Artemis IV in 2028.

item.title: NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public - WIRED
item.description:
NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.

Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.

The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

item.title: Life after the moon: Artemis II's Christina Koch steps down from active astronaut duty - Space
item.description:
Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon.

On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1.

"With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday.

Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future.

Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover, both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier. Glover will also work full-time at his alma mater, the California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) in San Luis Obispo.

"I'm grateful they will continue sharing what they learned with our astronauts, flight controllers and engineers as we prepare for Artemis III in 2027 and the missions that follow," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said of Wiseman and Glover in a Sept. 9 statement.

The fourth Artemis II astronaut, mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency, announced a change of his own in July: He planned to become a reservist in the Royal Canadian Air Force, where he's also a colonel. That move became official last month as well.

Artemis II sent the four astronauts on a 10-day trip around the moon in an Orion capsule. It was the first crewed mission of NASA's Artemis program and the first human spaceflight beyond low Earth orbit (LEO) since Apollo 17 in 1972.

As Isaacman mentioned, the next mission in the program is Artemis III, a docking test in LEO scheduled to launch next year. The Artemis III crew, which was announced in June, consists of NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik (commander), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (mission specialists) andLuca Parmitano of the European Space Agency (pilot).

If all goes according to plan, Artemis IV will land astronauts near the moon's south pole in 2028. We don't yet know who will fly on that historic mission.

Koch will succeed current NASA Deputy Chief Engineer Katherine Van Hooser, who will retire on Oct. 21 after more than 35 years of work for the space agency.

"In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA's engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency's programs and projects," agency officials said in Tuesday's statement.

Koch is a natural choice for the job, given her education and experience. She holds bachelor's degrees in electrical engineering and physics and a master's in electrical engineering, and she began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.

NASA selected Koch as an astronaut candidate in 2013. She has two spaceflights under her belt: Artemis II and a 328-day-flight to the International Space Station that launched in March 2019. That's the longest space mission ever conducted by a woman, and it featured the first three all-female spacewalks, which Koch conducted with fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Meir.

"Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space," Isaacman said in the Tuesday statement.

"After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role," he added. "I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. item.title: See more sights and sounds from the Artemis II moon mission - Scientific American
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II mission—a slingshot around the moon earlier this year that sent four astronauts to lunar space for the first time in more than half a century—was an unequivocal success. The voyage was chiefly a technological stepping stone for future crewed forays to the lunar surface, which should culminate with the founding of a small base near the moon’s south pole. But it was also a chance to carry out novel observations of the lunar farside, a largely mysterious realm that has been rarely glimpsed by human eyes.

Although Artemis II’s Orion spacecraft carried minimal science payloads, its astronauts were equipped with digital cameras (and iPhones)—and between April 1 and 10, they captured 814 gigabytes of lunar science data. At a press conference yesterday NASA presented its preliminary findings, which touch on everything from the moon’s surprisingly colorful craters to a series of curious flashes that the astronauts spied in lunar shadows. The release also includes more than eight hours of audio from the crew, videos of their nail-biting return to Earth, hand-annotated images, and much more—all available in a vast online repository.

Besides being breathtaking, the mission’s high-resolution imagery helps address more pragmatic queries: Which landing sites might be best for upcoming missions, and how safe would an outpost somewhere on the lunar farside be? “These findings are going to help shape future Artemis mission architectures,” said Marie Henderson, Artemis II’s deputy lunar science lead, during the press conference.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The crew’s sojourn around the moon may have been brief—just under seven hours—but they still surveyed a large swath of the farside, some of which was cloaked in total darkness. Arguably, the mission’s most important discovery emerged from those shadowy regions: five flashes of light, each in a different location on the lunar farside.

These were meteorite impacts. That isn’t inherently surprising: the airless moon gets bombarded by cosmic debris all the time. Sometimes these impactors—either asteroids or cometary fragments—are relatively big: in the spring of 2024, for example, a 15-meter object slammed into the moon with the force of an atomic bomb, cutting out a 222-meter-long pit.

Mostly, though, the moon is pelted by meteoroids the size of bullets or footballs. Each could, with a direct strike, kill an astronaut or trash a fancy new moon rover, so it’s good to know how often these small-but-lethal space rocks rain down on the lunar surface.

That’s why understanding what the Artemis II crew saw on the farside “matters for the future of human exploration,” said Jen Heldmann, a member of Artemis II’s lunar science team and deputy project scientist for Artemis IV, at the press event. Based on the brightness and brevity of the five flashes, scientists think each meteoroid was around 8.5 grams in mass—about as much as two dice. That may seem harmless, but they were moving at tens of kilometers per second, so these impactors are akin to space bullets.

The Artemis II crew flew outside any major annual meteoroid streams, meaning the five impacts they saw in just under an hour likely represent the typical background rate of small meteorite impacts on the lunar surface. With that in mind, NASA gauged the likelihood for a similar space bullet striking a future moon base: about a one-in-10,000 chance per decade. “We’re probably safe going forward,” Heldmann said.

The astronauts were also on the lookout for swarms of lunar dust. This jagged microscopic debris, easily dispersed by meteorite impacts and rocket exhaust, is corrosive, abrasive and adhesive. It makes quick work of wires, space suits and other hardware, chewing through them like space piranhas. Everyone hates it; it’s a major long-term hazard.

During the Apollo moon missions of the 1960s and 1970s, astronauts occasionally reported seeing hazes of sunlight-lofted dust drifting over parts of the lunar surface. But the Artemis II crew didn’t see any, suggesting that this strange phenomenon may be a transient problem rather than a persistent one.

The Artemis II images also revealed the subtle colors of lunar geology, showing that the moon’s seemingly monochrome surface is actually dappled with greens, yellows, grays and browns. Each of these hues, NASA’s analysis confirms, correspond to different types of ancient volcanism, from glasslike oozes to rubbly pyroclastic flow deposits. NASA also hoped that the crew could spy tectonic landforms during their flyby—things like faults, including those that could rupture and create prolonged, and potentially structure-toppling, moonquakes.

At one point, the crew caught a surreal series of arching crevasses in Oceanus Procellarum (the “Ocean of Storms,” a huge basin filled with primeval lava). These were wrinkle ridges, thought to form when the weight of the erupted lava squashes down on the moon’s crust, causing it to snap and contract. “The fact that they were able to see that from orbit was pretty phenomenal,” says Debra Needham, a member of the Artemis II science operations team.

Despite the fanfare of an official press conference, in truth, nothing in NASA’s report is especially revelatory. If anything, it serves as a reminder that unlocking the moon’s secrets—its alien geology, its hazardous landscapes and any scientific or economic treasures it may hold—relies getting a closer, surface-level look via more crewed and robotic investigations. In late September NASA also announced three new science payloads for near-future landings, all building on Artemis II’s success and adding to the case for an eventual moon base. One will monitor micrometeor impacts and other environmental threats at the lunar south pole, a second will search for hollow “lava tubes” that could be sites for underground habitats and a third will study how water ice might accumulate in and change the stability of lunar soil.

The report’s emphasis on future exploration was also tempered by an intentional callback to the past. NASA officials noted that their report’s release date, October 7, has significance in spaceflight history: on this day, back in 1959, the Soviet Union’s Luna 3 space probe beamed back the first-ever images of the moon’s farside, showing it to be a heavily scarred, crater-filled wasteland.

Luna 3’s images were eye-opening but still blandly colorless and fuzzy—especially compared with the kaleidoscopic, panchromatic views from Artemis II’s lunar pirouette. The alluring vistas the astronauts captured on digital cameras and iPhones helped ensure that “the entire world was united around our mission, and our crew,” says Kelsey Young, Artemis II’s lunar science lead. If NASA sticks to its plan and voyages to the moon become commonplace, then extraordinary images like these will quickly become glorious in their ordinariness.

item.title: John Larsen on writing 'Earthrise,' Jeremy Hansen's inside account of Artemis II - collectSPACE.com
item.description:
October 27, 2026

— John Larsen has not flown to the moon, but in his new book he chronicles the personal story of the first such journey in more than 50 years. In "Earthrise," a Canadian becomes the first person from outside the United States to launch to the moon. The flight offers views of the lunar far side never seen before by human eyes, including those of a first-time flyer who was experiencing spaceflight for the first time. "I didn't know him. He was 10 years younger than me, so we didn't really cross paths, but I had heard that a fighter pilot had been selected for the Artemis II mission and I was curious and interested in that," said Larsen, who spent 34 years serving in the Royal Canadian Air Force. That was three years ago. After seeing Jeremy Hansen on a late night talk show and getting a sense for his humility and sense of humor, Larsen decided to reach out to the Canadian Space Agency. "I had no contacts, but I pitched the book. I'd done a lot of writing and have the military connections, and that's what I think it would take to tell the story properly," said Larsen, who was a senior military public affairs officer and published author. As it turned out, it did not take much to convince the agency, and in turn Hansen, to get on board. "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" (or as in Canada, "A Canadian Astronaut's Journey Into Deep Space") was released by HarperCollins on Tuesday (Oct. 27). The following interview has been edited for length and clarity. collectSPACE (cS): The byline on the cover of "Earthrise" reads John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen, however, the book is written in part in Hansen's voice. Can you clarify for readers who wrote it? John Larsen: "The book itself. overall, is a composite. About half of it is in first-person voice, Jeremy's voice, and the other half is in third person. "Having said that, I wrote every word. I represented Jeremy's perspectives and thoughts in the first person. It was a collaboration between he and I, and the reason for that is when we crafted this deal with the Canadian Space Agency — who were supportive of the book being produced — they were very, very clear that Jeremy was mission centric, that he was planning to go to the moon and did not have time to be writing anything. "So I cast his words on the page for him in those sections." cS: How often did you speak with Jeremy during his training for the flight? Was it all by phone and email, or did you also travel to Johnson Space Center in Houston to meet with him? Larsen: "I met Jeremy for the first time in the summer of 2024 at his cottage up here in Canada, where I interviewed him and his family. A year later, I came down to Johnson for three days of media briefings and had a chance to talk to him again, as well as his flight directors and his crewmates. "On average, though, every couple of weeks I spent an hour or so with Jeremy on the phone. As we got later in the process, once he came back from the mission, almost the entire back third of the book was written in about five weeks. I devoted about 15 hours per day, every day and Jeremy was heavily engaged in that because I really needed to draw on his expertise and get his impressions about the mission." cS: Who else did you speak with as part of your research for the book? Larsen: "In terms of getting Jeremy's backstory, I spoke to his teachers from when he was in school. He was very active in the air cadet program. That's how he got his pilot's license. I took the same path. I was an air cadet. I got a pilot's license too, so I could relate to that trajectory. We did it in different parts of the country, but it's a similar program. I talked to his cadet officers, and then at one point, I drove to the other side of Toronto and met his parents — wonderful, wonderful people. I really tried to get a sense of who was this man, what was his constitution, his core being, before he even put his name into the hat to become an astronaut. I thought it was a very important part of the story to tell." cS: Did you have any contact with Jeremy during the mission? Did he email you from space? Larsen: "There would only have been one opportunity for me to do that and that was at the Canadian Space Agency in Montreal. I discussed that with with officials at the CSA, and we mutually agreed that I already had tons of access to him so I was happy enough just to draw from what he was saying to others. For example, our prime minister talked with Jeremy and with school children during the mission, so I pulled from that. "We did reconnect as soon as he came back. In fact, it was either late that evening or very, very early the following morning that I got a text from him that literally said, 'Hey, I'm back.' That's it. I laughed, and replied, 'Yeah, dude, I know.' But it just goes to show the humility of the man that he thought to send me a note letting me know he's back, and not that millions of people weren't watching the entire trip and knew every element of the reentry, splashdown and recovery. "Then we were very closely connected for the next five weeks because I had to file the final 30,000 words or so. I had to get his story and then he had to edit it. There were a lot of technical details, particularly where we go into some of the elements of the trip that were unexpected — and there were unexpected elements. I wanted to make sure I captured those authentically and properly." cS: Of all of the things that happened during the mission, what struck you as being the really great stories you wanted to include in the book? Larsen: "We saw four astronauts who were real human beings. They weren't the stereotypical cigar chomping, whiskey drinking fighter pilots of the 1960s. They were highly evolved, emotional human beings who weren't reluctant to show that, and that's what I think people gravitated to. "Obviously, the mission itself was a great adventure, but that's not what drew people in. What drew people in is they saw this humanity. I heard somebody refer to them the other day as 'our emotional support astronauts,' and that's almost what happened. I think Jeremy captured it beautifully, and I'm paraphrasing it a bit here, but he said something to the effect of, 'If you liked what you saw up there in space over the last 10 days, and my sense is a lot of you did, look at yourselves. We all have this capacity within ourselves. It's all in you.' "I think that ability to be self-reflective and asking people to do that was very powerful. "And then, of course, the moment I think that just got me, and it got everybody, and it's exactly what I'm talking about here, was the moment the crew named the crater on the moon after Reid [Wiseman, the mission commander's] wife who passed. They had planned to do it, but I think the raw energy of the moment and authenticity of the moment, it just took everybody's breath away." cS: So what do you hope readers take away from reading "Earthrise"? Larsen: "Honestly, believe in humanity. Believe in the great things we can do when we come together. It was always a message behind the mission, but I think it really came to life when people saw it. It was one of the few experiences in the last year that transcended geopolitical boundaries, that joined us as humans — as spaceflight has always intended to do and as it has in the past. We needed it. We needed it at this point in time. "The second thing is a more personal message, which is around finding joy. Find joy in what you're doing. We live our lives and they are often very hectic, and sometimes they're infused with acrimony and dissent. It doesn't mean it's always going to be easy, but you need to have a sense of joy in what you're doing. "I think those are the takeaways. And it's ironic, isn't it? Because neither of those messages are about space exploration, itself."

item.title: NASA shares Artemis II astronauts’ handwritten mission notes - Popular Science
item.description:
Successfully sending Artemis II astronauts on their historic lunar flyby earlier this year required some of the latest and most precise technologies, but not everything in this mission needed the same intense equipment. As crewmates gazed through Orion’s capsule window at the moon’s eclipse of the sun on April 6, 2026, three of the travelers needed a way to easily sketch some of their preliminary observations. They took turns writing their notes on a shared tablet PC—and NASA has recently highlighted their work with a screenshot of their efforts.

Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen had a lengthy list of tasks during their 10-day, 700,000-mile roundtrip. One of the most visually dramatic jobs involved carefully assessing lunar activity while passing across the moon’s dark side from a distance of about 46,000 miles away. The roughly hour-long observation period provided astronauts with an unprecedented opportunity to record meteorite activity.

A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet. Credit: NASA

The tablet screenshot includes notes taken by Wisemen (in blue), Hansen (in red), and Glover (in green) during the moon’s eclipse of the sun. The crew collectively spotted at least five faint flashes of light caused by impacts. According to Wiseman, the first three impacts occurred within about 10 minutes into their observations, while another two happened later during the flyby. Impacts two and four were likely also corroborated by Hansen and Glover.

Since the moon does not have an atmosphere like Earth’s, the lunar surface is regularly bombarded by space rocks. Most of them are comparatively small, but they will still pose a problem for future crewed trips to the surface,especially those stationed in a planned permanent lunar base. The data gathered by Artemis II on April 6 will help NASA better understand these dynamics, and plan for the safest environments possible for their astronauts.

Artemis II’s astronauts safely returned to Earth during a splashdown off the coast of San Diego at 8:07 p.m. EDT on April 11. If all goes as planned, Artemis III’s crew will launch on their mission no earlier than June 2027.

item.title: 'Let's all choose to make tomorrow better', Artemis II astronauts honored with Stephen Hawking Medal at Starmus - Space
item.description:
TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — The Artemis II astronauts may have traveled hundreds of thousands of miles away from Earth to the moon, but they made sure the rest of us didn't miss out on the adventure.

Now, their efforts to bring the wonders of space exploration back down to Earth have earned them one of science communication's most prestigious honors: the Stephen Hawking Medal.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover, alongside Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, accepted the award on Saturday (Oct. 17), during the opening ceremony of the Starmus VIII festival. The honor recognizes all four crew members, including NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who wasn't in attendance.

For Wiseman, the experience of seeing our home planet from the vicinity of the moon carried a powerful message.

"If we could take each of you 250,000 miles away from this planet, 400,000 kilometers away from planet Earth, and you would see Earth the size of your thumb. It's tiny," Wiseman told the audience.

"When you're there looking through the moon, back at this tiny Earth, the only thing you feel is love, peace, hope, unity", he continued. "Those aren't the right words, but that is all you feel."

During their historic Artemis II mission, the astronauts did far more than put NASA's Orion spacecraft through its paces. Through live communications, interviews and glimpses into life aboard the spacecraft, not to mention the jaw-dropping photos that just keep on coming, they helped turn an extraordinarily complex mission into something people worldwide could experience and connect with.

And that's exactly what the Stephen Hawking Medal is designed to celebrate.

Established in 2016 by physicist Stephen Hawking and Starmus, the award honors those who have gone above and beyond to make science accessible, engaging and inspiring.

The Artemis II crew joins some pretty impressive company. Previous recipients include Apollo 11 moonwalker Buzz Aldrin, naturalist David Attenborough, primatologist Jane Goodall and astrophysicist Neil DeGrasse Tyson.

This year's ceremony marks the medal's 10th anniversary, with filmmaker Ridley Scott also among the 2026 honourees.

"It's a special thrill for us at Starmus to be able to honor the intrepid Artemis II crew members in the same way that we honored the Apollo astronauts who paved the way to the moon over 50 years ago," Starmus co-founder and Queen guitarist Brian May said in a statement ahead of the ceremony.

Wiseman left the audience with one final thought.

"When you come home to this beautiful planet, you realise that it's in every single one of us to choose to make tomorrow better," he said. "So let's all choose to make tomorrow better".

Starmus VIII runs from Oct. 17-22 across Tenerife and La Palma in the Canary Islands. This year's festival, themed "The Search for Truth", brings together leading scientists, astronauts, musicians and artists to celebrate scientific discovery and explore the importance of evidence and scientific thinking.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

item.title: NASA Welcomes Record-Setting Artemis II Moonfarers Back to Earth - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
The first astronauts to travel to the Moon in more than half a century are back on Earth after a record-setting mission aboard NASA’s Artemis II test flight.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen splashed down at 5:07 p.m. PDT Friday off the coast of San Diego, completing a nearly 10-day journey that took them 252,756 miles from home at their farthest distance from Earth.

“Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy, welcome home, and congratulations on a truly historic achievement. NASA is grateful to President Donald Trump and partners in Congress for providing the mandate and resources that made this mission and the future of Artemis possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Artemis II demonstrated extraordinary skill, courage, and dedication as the crew pushed Orion, SLS (Space Launch System), and human exploration farther than ever before. As the first astronauts to fly this rocket and spacecraft, the crew accepted significant risk in service of the knowledge gained and the future we are determined to build. NASA also acknowledges the contributions of the entire NASA workforce, along with our international partners, whose expertise and commitment were essential to this mission’s success. With Artemis II complete, focus now turns confidently toward assembling Artemis III and preparing to return to the lunar surface, build the base, and never give up the Moon again.”

After splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, the astronauts were met by a combined NASA and U.S. military team that assisted them out of the spacecraft in open water and transported them via helicopter to the USS John P. Murtha for initial medical checkouts. The crew members are expected to return to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston on Saturday, April 11.

During their mission, Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen flew 694,481 miles in total. Their lunar flyby took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before, surpassing the previous distance record set by Apollo 13 astronauts in 1970.

The first Artemis crew launched on NASA’s SLS rocket at 6:35 p.m. April 1, from Launch Pad 39B at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. With 8.8 million pounds of thrust at liftoff, the American-built rocket propelled the crew inside the Orion spacecraft to space, delivering it to orbit with pinpoint accuracy after a smooth countdown conducted by the agency’s Artemis launch control team.

During the first day in space, the astronauts and teams on the ground checked out the spacecraft — named Integrity by the crew — to confirm all systems were healthy ahead of the transit to the Moon. NASA also deployed four CubeSats from international partners to Earth orbit.

On the second day of the test flight, with all systems Go, Orion’s service module fired its main engine, placing the astronauts on a trajectory that brought them 4,067 miles above the lunar surface at their closest approach.

“The Artemis II crew is home. The entry, descent, and landing systems performed as designed and the final test was completed as intended. This moment belongs to the thousands of people across fourteen countries who built, tested, and trusted this vehicle. Their work protected four human lives traveling at 25,000 miles per hour and brought them safely back to Earth,” said NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya. “Artemis II proved the vehicle, the teams, the architecture, and the international partnership that will return humanity to the lunar surface. Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy carried the hopes of this world farther than humans have traveled in more than half a century. Fifty‑three years ago, humanity left the Moon. This time, we returned to stay. The future is ours to win.”

With astronauts aboard for the first time, engineers put Orion through a full in‑flight evaluation. The crew tested the spacecraft’s life support systems, confirming Orion can sustain humans in deep space. During several piloting demonstrations, crew members took manual control of the spacecraft, flying Orion to validate its handling and collect data that will guide future rendezvous and docking operations with human-rated landers during Artemis III and beyond.

The crew completed a series of tests to inform how NASA will fly future missions to the Moon, including evaluations of how the spacecraft operates during crew exercise, emergency equipment and procedures, the Orion crew survival system spacesuits, and other critical spacecraft systems.

Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen also supported scientific investigations to help NASA prepare astronauts to live and work on the Moon as the agency builds a Moon Base and looks toward Mars. These experiments — including the AVATAR investigation, which studies how human tissue responds to microgravity and the deep space radiation environment, and other human research performance studies — are gathering essential health data for long-duration missions.

During their April 6 lunar flyby, the astronauts captured more than 7,000 images of the lunar surface and a solar eclipse, during which the Moon blocked the Sun from Orion’s vantage point. The imagery includes striking views of earthset and earthrise, impact craters, ancient lava flows, our Milky Way galaxy, and surface fractures and color variations across the lunar terrain.

They documented the topography along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — where low-angle sunlight casts long shadows across the surface, creating illumination conditions similar to those in the South Pole region where astronauts are scheduled to land in 2028. The crew also proposed potential names for two lunar craters and reported meteoroid impact flashes on the night side of the Moon.

Artemis II science will pave the way for future missions to the Moon’s surface by helping advance mission operations and training astronauts to use well-informed judgment to identify areas of high interest for science and exploration.

With the crew safely on Earth, NASA and its partners now will turn attention to preparing for next year’s Artemis III mission, when a new Orion crew will test integrated operations with commercially built Moon landers in low Earth orbit.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly challenging missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and lay the groundwork for sending the first astronauts – American astronauts – to Mars.

To learn more about the Artemis program, visit:
